title: Cap. VIII Arg.: if God reprobates from himself, fewer reprobates than predestined (Ps. 145:9; Gregory of Valencia)
latin: Sic argutantur quidam: Si Deus non propter peccata hominum, sed sua sponte et ex seipso, homines reprobaret, tum pauciores essent reprobati quam praedestinati. Nam Deus longe propensior est ex se ad miserendum et benefaciendum hominibus, quam ad deserendos, perdendos, et damnandos, juxta illud Psalmi, Psal. cxlv. 9. Suavis Dominus universis, et miserationes ejus super omnia opera ejus. Hanc rationem Gregorius de Valentia (ex quo pleraque superiora argumenta desumpsimus) suo judicio optimam esse pronunciat, eamque se a Joanne Fekio mutuatam fuisse profitetur.
pass_a: So some argue: If God were to reprobate men not on account of the sins of men, but of his own accord and from himself, then there would be fewer reprobated than predestined. For God is far more inclined from himself unto having mercy and doing good unto men, than unto deserting, destroying, and damning them, according to that of the Psalm, Psalm 145:9. The Lord is sweet unto all, and his compassions are over all his works. This reason Gregory of Valencia (from whom we have taken most of the superior arguments) pronounces in his judgment to be the best, and professes that it was borrowed by him from John Fekius.
pass_b: Some argue thus: if God reprobated men not for their sins, but of his own accord and from himself, then there would be fewer reprobate than predestined. For God is far more inclined from himself to mercy and beneficence than to deserting, destroying, and damning — according to Psalm 145:9: The Lord is sweet to all, and his compassions are over all his works. Gregory of Valencia (from whom we have taken most of the earlier arguments) judges this the best reason, and says he borrowed it from John Fekius.

lemmas.gloss: fewer reprobates than predestined if from self

title: Cap. VIII Resp.: same consequence fails for election and reprobation; negative reprobation is denial of unowed benefit
latin: Hanc eandem rationem a Gregorio propositam in quaestione Praedestinationis antea dissolvimus. Nam in illa controversia conatus est probare, praedestinationem esse ex praescientia operum, quia pauci electi sunt respectu rejectorum. Jam etiam contendit, reprobationem pendere ex praevisione finalium demeritorum, quia multi sunt reprobati in comparatione ad eos paucos qui eliguntur. Respondeo igitur, consequentiam neutrobi valere. Ad reprobationem quod spectat, cum sit (ut ante dictum est) non punitio, sed gratuiti et indebiti beneficii negatio, nihil cogit nos fateri Deum, ex mero suo beneplacito agentem, non posse tale beneficium paucioribus concedere, et pluribus denegare. Videmus in angelis hoc beneficium electionis fuisse multis negatum, idque absque respectu ad praevisa demerita: an fuerit pluribus denegatum quam indultum, haud ausim definire. Si tamen in ipsa re aliquid esset incongruum, aut Deo indignum, non modo pluribus, sed nec paucioribus, imo nec uni posset hoc beneficium electionis denegare absque consideratione praevisi peccati. Hac igitur sola instantia vis argumenti eliditur.
pass_a: This same reason proposed by Gregory we dissolved before in the question of Predestination. For in that controversy he tried to prove that predestination is from foresight of works, because few are elect in respect of the rejected. Now he also contends that reprobation hangs upon foresight of final demerits, because many are reprobated in comparison unto those few who are elected. I answer therefore that the consequence avails in neither place. As to what regards reprobation, since it is (as was said before) not punishment, but the negation of a gratuitous and unowed benefit, nothing compels us to confess that God, acting from his mere good pleasure, cannot grant such a benefit to fewer, and deny it to more. We see in the angels that this benefit of election was denied to many, and that without respect unto foresighted demerits: whether it was denied to more than was granted, I scarce dare define. Yet if in the thing itself anything were incongruous, or unworthy of God, he could deny this benefit of election not only not to more, but not even to fewer, nay not even to one, without consideration of foresighted sin. By this sole instance therefore the force of the argument is broken.
pass_b: We already dissolved this same reason of Gregory's in the predestination question. There he tried to prove predestination is from foresight of works because few are elect relative to the rejected. Now he contends reprobation hangs on foresight of final demerits because many are reprobate compared with the few elect. I answer: the consequence holds in neither place. As for reprobation — since it is not punishment but denial of a gratuitous unowed benefit — nothing forces us to say God, acting from mere good pleasure, cannot grant that benefit to fewer and deny it to more. We see in the angels that this benefit of election was denied to many, and without regard to foresighted demerits; whether denied to more than granted, I scarce dare say. Yet if anything in the thing itself were incongruous or unworthy of God, he could not deny election's benefit even to one without regard to foresighted sin — let alone to many. That single instance breaks the argument's force.

lemmas.gloss: fails for both election and reprobation counts
angels: election denied without foresight demerit

title: Cap. VIII Resp.: human mass of merited damnation; Augustine De bono persever. 8; Rom. 9:20
latin: Sed ab angelis ad homines descendamus. Dico igitur in hominibus hujus rei aequitatem multo facilius perspici posse quam in angelis. Nam cum universa massa humani generis in statum meritae damnationis defluxerit primi parentis nostri inobedientia, si Deus nullo ulteriore ad peccata actualia respectu praeterire et rejicere velit quamvis multos in praeparatione et donatione gratiae specialis, praeterit et rejicit eos, in quibus nihil invenit propter quod ad tam eximium beneficium participandum eligantur, et in quibus multa invenit propter quae tali beneficio indignissimi censeantur. Nihil aliud hic dicendum restat praeter illud Augustini, Qui liberatur, gratiam diligat; qui non liberatur, debitum agnoscat, De bono persever. cap. 8. Et illud Apostoli, Rom. ix. 20. O homo, tu quis es qui respondeas Deo? Num dicet figmentum, etc.
pass_a: But let us descend from angels unto men. I say therefore that in men the equity of this matter can be much more easily perceived than in angels. For since the universal mass of the human race has flowed down into the state of merited damnation by the disobedience of our first parent, if God with no further respect unto actual sins wills to pass by and reject howsoever many in the preparation and donation of special grace, he passes by and rejects those in whom he finds nothing on account of which they should be elected unto participating in so excellent a benefit, and in whom he finds many things on account of which they are judged most unworthy of such a benefit. Nothing else remains to be said here besides that of Augustine, Let him who is freed love grace; let him who is not freed acknowledge the debt, On the Good of Perseverance chapter 8. And that of the Apostle, Rom. 9:20. O man, who art thou that answerest God? Shall the thing formed say, etc.
pass_b: Descend from angels to men. In men the equity of this is far easier to see. Since the whole mass of humankind has flowed down into merited damnation by our first parent's disobedience, if God with no further regard to actual sins wills to pass by and reject however many in preparing and giving special grace, he passes by and rejects those in whom he finds nothing for which they should be elect to so excellent a benefit, and in whom he finds much for which they are most unworthy of it. Nothing else need be said but Augustine (On the Good of Perseverance 8): Let him who is freed love grace; let him who is not freed acknowledge the debt — and Paul (Rom. 9:20): O man, who are you to answer God? Shall the thing formed say...?

lemmas.lemma: De bono persever. cap. 8 / Rom. ix. 20
lemmas.gloss: love grace or acknowledge debt; clay/potter

title: Cap. VIII Resp.: propensity to mercy need not give special grace to most; praeterition is not desertion
latin: Sed Deus propensior est ex se ad miserendum et benefaciendum hominibus, quam ad eos deserendos et perdendos. Concedimus. At qui est propensissimus ad miserendum et benefaciendum, non solet eximia et peculiaria beneficia aut omnibus aut pluribus impertiri. Sufficit ad hanc propensionem Dei in misericordiam ostendendam, quod omnium misereatur quoad multa misericordiae suae effecta, quamvis quoad hoc speciale effectum, gratiam specialem praeparandi et ad vitam aeternam infallibiliter ordinandi, nec omnium nec plurium misereatur. Dein praeterire vel reprobare non est idem quod deserere et perdere. Deseruntur quidem et perduntur tandem omnes reprobati sive non-electi: sed quod praeteriti fuerint aut non-electi ad gratiam specialem, ex mera Dei voluntate prodit; quod autem postmodum deserti et perditi, ex interveniente illorum demerito originem sumpsit. Hactenus iis argumentis satisfecimus quibus utitur Gregorius de Valentia, in 1. Aquinat. qu. 23. de Reprobatione.
pass_a: But God is more inclined from himself unto having mercy and doing good unto men, than unto deserting and destroying them. We grant it. But he who is most inclined unto having mercy and doing good is not wont to impart excellent and peculiar benefits either unto all or unto most. It suffices unto showing this propensity of God unto mercy, that he has mercy on all as to many effects of his mercy, although as to this special effect, of preparing special grace and of infallibly ordaining unto eternal life, he has mercy neither on all nor on most. Then to pass by or to reprobate is not the same as to desert and to destroy. Indeed all the reprobated or non-elect are at length deserted and destroyed: but that they were passed by or non-elect unto special grace proceeds from the mere will of God; but that afterward they were deserted and destroyed took origin from their intervening demerit. Thus far we have satisfied those arguments which Gregory of Valencia uses, on 1 of Aquinas, question 23, concerning Reprobation.
pass_b: But God is more inclined from himself to mercy and beneficence than to deserting and destroying men. We grant it. Yet the most merciful is not wont to impart excellent peculiar benefits to all or even to most. It is enough to show that propensity that he has mercy on all as to many effects of his mercy — even if, as to this special effect of preparing special grace and infallibly ordaining to eternal life, he has mercy neither on all nor on most. Further: to pass by or reprobate is not the same as to desert and destroy. Yes, all the reprobate or non-elect are at length deserted and destroyed — but that they were passed by or non-elect as to special grace proceeds from God's mere will; that afterward they were deserted and destroyed took its origin from their intervening demerit. So far we have answered the arguments Gregory of Valencia uses on Aquinas I, q. 23, on Reprobation.

lemmas.gloss: mercy propensity ≠ special grace to most
praeterition from will; desertion from demerit
